    How Oregon taxes a paycheck

    Oregon taxes wage income on a graduated scale, and the ladder is steep. ORS 316.037 imposes the tax and ORS 316.037(1)(a) sets the brackets: 4.75% on the first slice of taxable income, 6.75% above $4,550, 8.75% above $11,400, and 9.9% above $125,000 for a single filer in 2026. A married couple filing jointly reaches the same 9.9% top rate, but not until taxable income passes $250,000. That 9.9% is the fourth-highest top marginal rate in the country, behind California at 13.3%, Hawaii at 11%, and New Jersey at 10.75%. It is the highest rate Oregon has ever charged, and it is the single most important fact about an Oregon paycheck.

    Oregon also has no sales tax, so it leans hard on income and property taxes instead. Before the brackets apply, the calculator subtracts a standard deduction of $2,745 for a single filer, $5,490 for a married couple filing jointly, and $4,118 for a head of household. The dataset behind this page stores a simplified three-band version of the schedule — 4.75%, 7.325%, and 9.9% — which merges Oregon's middle 6.75% and 8.75% rates into a single band. The dataset is a deliberately rough approximation: at $70,000 it returns about $4,540, where the full statutory schedule would produce roughly $5,570. Treat the state line here as a conservative estimate, not a reproduction of the Department of Revenue withholding tables.

    The Portland metro area adds a tax that no other part of Oregon pays. Two separate measures create local personal income taxes on residents. Multnomah County voters approved the Preschool for All tax in 2020, and it applies to Multnomah County residents alone. Regional voters approved the Metro supportive housing services tax in 2020, and that one covers residents of Multnomah, Washington, and Clackamas counties. Both are collected by the Oregon Department of Revenue alongside the state return, and both are charged as a percentage of taxable income above a high threshold, so a Multnomah County resident who owes both can face a combined marginal rate above 11%. The calculator on this page reports the state tax only and does not add either local tax.

    How Oregon take-home pay is calculated

    1. Start with gross pay for the period. A $70,000 salary paid biweekly is $2,692.31 before any deduction.
    2. Subtract pre-tax elections first. A 401(k), HSA, or health premium reduces federal taxable income, and because Oregon starts its own calculation from federal taxable income, the same contribution lowers the Oregon bill too.
    3. Subtract federal income tax, withheld under the IRS percentage method for your filing status and the elections on your Form W-4.
    4. Subtract Social Security at 6.2% of gross pay up to the annual wage base ($184,500 for 2026) and Medicare at 1.45% of all gross pay, plus the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax above $200,000 of wages.
    5. Apply Oregon income tax. Subtract the $2,745 single-filer standard deduction, then run the remainder through the graduated brackets. This calculator uses the dataset's three-band approximation of 4.75%, 7.325%, and 9.9%, so a salary near a band edge can differ slightly from a payroll system that uses the Department of Revenue tables.
    6. Oregon Paid Leave and transit withholding. Two more state lines come out of Oregon wages but are not yet subtracted here: the Paid Leave Oregon premium at 0.6% of wages up to $184,500, and the statewide transit tax at 0.1% of wages with no cap.
    7. Subtract nothing for a local income tax unless you live in Multnomah, Washington, or Clackamas County, where the Preschool for All and supportive housing services taxes apply. Neither is modeled here.
    8. The remainder is net take-home pay for that period.

    The result is your net pay for the period you selected. Pay frequency matters: a biweekly schedule pays 26 times a year and a semi-monthly schedule 24, so the same salary produces different per-paycheck amounts.

    Worked example: $70,000 in Oregon

    A single filer earning $70,000 a year, paid bi-weekly in 2026:

    LinePer paycheck
    Gross pay$2,692.31
    Federal income tax$252.69
    Social Security$166.92
    Medicare$39.04
    Oregon state income tax$174.62
    Net take-home pay$2,059.03

    That is $53,534.82 a year, an effective tax rate of about 23.5%. Change the inputs in the calculator above to see your own numbers.

    How Oregon compares

    Oregon sits at the opposite end of the income-tax spectrum from its eastern neighbor Idaho. Idaho charges a flat 5.695%, less than Oregon's 6.75% second band, and Idaho runs no local income tax anywhere in the state. Washington, directly to the north, has no wage income tax at all, which is why a Portland worker commuting to Vancouver takes home meaningfully more than the same salary earned in Portland. Nevada and Wyoming, two more no-tax states, sit further east along the same Interstate 80 corridor. At $70,000 a single Oregon filer pays about $4,540 a year in state income tax, where the same salary in Washington would pay nothing and in Idaho would pay roughly $3,160.

    What makes Oregon unusual among high-tax states is the local layer, and it exists in only one corner of the state. California, New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Maryland, and Indiana all levy local income taxes, but Oregon's apply to just three counties around Portland. A resident of those counties pays the state rate plus the county rate, so the combined marginal rate on high income can exceed 11%. A resident of Eugene, Bend, Medford, or Salem pays the state rate alone, because no other Oregon county has adopted a local personal income tax.

    Oregon also withholds two smaller payroll amounts that a no-tax state does not. Paid Leave Oregon, created by HB 2005 in 2019, is funded by a premium of 1% of gross wages up to the Social Security wage base of $184,500, and the employee pays 60% of that, or 0.6% of wages. The employer pays the other 40% only if it averages 25 or more employees; a smaller employer withholds the employee share but pays nothing itself. Separately, the statewide transit tax withholds 0.1% of wages from every Oregon worker, resident or not, to fund public transit, and it has no wage cap. On $70,000 the two together take about $490 a year, or roughly $18.85 per biweekly paycheck, on top of the state income tax shown above.

    Oregon's rate ladder is also unusual for how low it starts. The 4.75% first band covers only the first $4,550 of taxable income, then the rate jumps to 6.75% and again to 8.75% at just $11,400. Most states with a top rate near 10% hold their lower bands for far more income. The practical effect is that a modest Oregon salary reaches a mid-single-digit marginal rate quickly, and the 9.9% top rate arrives at $125,000 of taxable income, a level many two-earner Oregon households cross. Oregon does soften the load for low earners with a state earned income credit and a retirement income credit, but both are claimed on the annual return and change nothing on a paycheck.

    FAQ

    What is the Oregon income tax rate for 2026?

    Oregon uses graduated brackets under ORS 316.037(1)(a). For a single filer the 2026 rates are 4.75% on taxable income up to $4,550, 6.75% above $4,550, 8.75% above $11,400, and 9.9% above $125,000. A married couple filing jointly uses the same rates with doubled thresholds, reaching 9.9% above $250,000. That 9.9% is the fourth-highest top rate in the country, behind California, Hawaii, and New Jersey.

    How much is taken out of a $70,000 salary in Oregon?

    For 2026, a single filer paid biweekly takes home about $2,059.03 per paycheck from a $70,000 salary: $2,692.31 gross, $252.69 federal income tax, $166.92 Social Security, $39.04 Medicare, and $174.62 Oregon state income tax. That is $53,534.82 a year, an effective tax rate of about 23.5%. The state figure uses this calculator's simplified three-band dataset, and it does not include the Paid Leave or transit withholding.

    Does Oregon have a local or county income tax?

    Yes, in the Portland area only, and under two separate measures. Multnomah County residents pay the Preschool for All personal income tax, approved by county voters in 2020. Residents of Multnomah, Washington, and Clackamas counties pay the Metro supportive housing services tax, approved by regional voters in 2020. Both are collected by the Oregon Department of Revenue and apply as a percentage of taxable income above a high threshold. No other Oregon county has adopted a local personal income tax, so residents of Eugene, Salem, Bend, or Medford pay the state rate alone.

    What is the Paid Leave Oregon deduction?

    Paid Leave Oregon is funded by a premium of 1% of gross wages up to the 2026 Social Security wage base of $184,500. Employees pay 60% of that premium, which is 0.6% of wages, and employers with 25 or more employees on average pay the remaining 40%. Employers with fewer than 25 employees withhold the employee share but pay no employer share. On a $70,000 salary the employee share is about $420 a year, or roughly $16.15 per biweekly paycheck.

    What is the Oregon statewide transit tax?

    It is a withholding tax of one-tenth of one percent, or 0.001, on wages, enacted by HB 2017 to fund public transit. Employers have withheld it since July 1, 2018 from the wages of Oregon residents regardless of where they work, and from nonresidents who perform services in Oregon. It has no wage cap, so it applies to every dollar of wages. On a $70,000 salary it comes to $70 a year, about $2.69 per biweekly paycheck.

    What is Oregon's standard deduction for 2026?

    The calculator on this page subtracts $2,745 for a single filer, $5,490 for a married couple filing jointly, and $4,118 for a head of household. Oregon indexes its standard deduction for inflation, so the published amount for the year can differ slightly from the figure used in this simplified dataset. Treat the Oregon line here as a close estimate rather than a reproduction of the Department of Revenue withholding tables.

    Does Oregon have a state disability insurance program?

    No. Oregon operates no state disability insurance program, so no SDI line appears on an Oregon paycheck. The state's only payroll insurance deduction is the Paid Leave Oregon premium of 0.6% of wages paid by the employee, which funds family and medical leave benefits rather than short-term disability.

    Does Oregon tax Social Security benefits?

    Oregon does not tax Social Security benefits. The state allows a subtraction for Social Security income included in federal taxable income, so those benefits are removed before the Oregon brackets are applied. Oregon also offers a retirement income credit for filers 62 and older whose household income falls below a threshold, claimed on the annual return rather than through payroll.
